title: c-ANCA and p-ANCA, Microscopic Polyangiitis, Churg-Strauss, and Buerger Disease

steps.tx: Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) are circulating autoantibodies directed against primary azurophilic granule enzymes of neutrophils and monocyte lysosomes. Diagnostic indirect immunofluorescence on ethanol-fixed normal human neutrophils resolves two distinct staining patterns: **cytoplasmic granular c-ANCA staining**, showing diffuse granular cytoplasmic fluorescence with central interlobular accentuation, and perinuclear p-ANCA staining, where artifactual basic antigen migration produces a rim of fluorescence encircling the nucleus. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays identify proteinase-3 (PR3) as the target of c-ANCA, and myeloperoxidase (MPO) as the target of p-ANCA.
steps.say: Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, or ANCAs, target enzymes inside neutrophil primary granules. When tested by indirect immunofluorescence on ethanol-fixed neutrophils, they produce two distinct patterns: c-ANCA shows diffuse speckled fluorescence throughout the cytoplasm, targeting proteinase-3. In contrast, p-ANCA displays a perinuclear ring of fluorescence around the nucleus, targeting myeloperoxidase. These antibodies activate neutrophils, causing them to release oxygen radicals and degranulate inside small blood vessels.

vis.alt: Immunofluorescence patterns of cytoplasmic c-ANCA versus perinuclear p-ANCA on ethanol-fixed human neutrophils

steps.tx: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, formerly known as Wegener granulomatosis, is a necrotizing systemic vasculitis defined by a classic clinical triad: necrotizing granulomas of the upper respiratory tract (recurrent sinusitis, nasal mucosal ulcerations, saddle-nose cartilage deformity), necrotizing granulomas of the lungs (bilateral cavitary pulmonary nodules and hemoptysis), and focal necrotizing **pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis**. Serum c-ANCA directed against proteinase-3 is positive in over ninety percent of active generalized disease, correlating closely with disease activity, with immunosuppression utilizing cyclophosphamide or rituximab inducing remission.
steps.say: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis characterized by a classic triad affecting the upper airways, lungs, and kidneys. Patients present with chronic sinusitis, nasal ulceration, and a sunken saddle-nose deformity from cartilage destruction. Chest imaging reveals bilateral cavitary lung nodules. Kidney biopsy demonstrates crescentic necrotizing glomerulonephritis with virtually no antibody deposition. Over ninety percent of patients test strongly positive for c-ANCA against proteinase-3.

left.title: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA)
points: Upper airway: Necrotizing granulomas (saddle-nose)
Lungs: Bilateral cavitary pulmonary nodules
Kidneys: Pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis
Serology: Strongly c-ANCA / PR3-positive (>90%)

right.title: Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA)
points: Upper airway: Strictly absent; no granulomas formed
Lungs: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage without cavities
Kidneys: Identical necrotizing crescentic GN
Serology: Strongly p-ANCA / MPO-positive (>75%)

steps.tx: Microscopic polyangiitis is a necrotizing systemic vasculitis affecting small vessels: post-capillary venules, capillaries, and arterioles. In sharp contrast to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, **granulomatous inflammation is completely absent** in microscopic polyangiitis, and upper respiratory tract disease does not occur. All lesions are typically of the same developmental age, showing transmural fibrinoid necrosis with prominent neutrophil karyorrhexis (leukocytoclasia). Clinical features are dominated by rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary capillaritis presenting with life-threatening diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, with seventy to eighty percent of patients testing positive for p-ANCA.
steps.say: Microscopic polyangiitis is a necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis that lacks granulomatous inflammation entirely. All lesions appear at the same chronological stage, demonstrating transmural fibrinoid necrosis and fragmented neutrophilic debris called leukocytoclasia. The primary clinical danger is pulmonary-renal syndrome, where alveolar capillaritis causes pulmonary hemorrhage and rapid crescentic renal failure. Over seventy percent of patients test positive for p-ANCA targeting myeloperoxidase.

vis.alt: Renal biopsy histology in microscopic polyangiitis showing pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis
vis.caption: Microscopic polyangiitis renal biopsy with crescentic glomerulonephritis.

steps.tx: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, historically termed Churg-Strauss syndrome, is an uncommon necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis classically evolving through three phases. The prodromal phase features allergic rhinitis and severe, late-onset bronchial asthma. The eosinophilic tissue phase displays marked **peripheral blood absolute eosinophilia** exceeding one thousand cells per microliter and eosinophilic tissue infiltrates in lungs and gut. The third phase is systemic necrotizing vasculitis with extravascular necrotizing granulomas. Approximately fifty percent of patients are p-ANCA positive, and eosinophilic myocardial infiltration with cardiomyopathy represents the leading cause of death.
steps.say: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, or Churg-Strauss syndrome, is a unique small-vessel vasculitis linked to severe allergic asthma. It begins with intractable asthma and allergic rhinitis, followed by marked peripheral blood eosinophilia. The disease culminates in systemic vasculitis with extravascular necrotizing granulomas rich in eosinophils. Peripheral nerves are frequently damaged, producing mononeuritis multiplex. The most dangerous complication is eosinophilic myocarditis, which is responsible for half of all deaths.

vis.alt: Clinical and histopathological manifestations of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
vis.caption: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis across lung, nerve, and skin.

steps.tx: In all three ANCA-associated vasculitides, renal involvement is defined histologically as **pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis**. Severe focal necrotizing inflammation disrupts glomerular capillary basement membranes, permitting plasma proteins, fibrin, and red cells to extravasate into the urinary Bowman space. Fibrin stimulates parietal epithelial cells and infiltrating monocytes to proliferate rapidly, forming multi-layered cellular crescents that compress and obliterate the glomerular capillary tuft. Crucially, direct immunofluorescence microscopy reveals a pauci-immune pattern (absence of significant IgG or complement deposition), distinguishing it from anti-GBM disease and lupus nephritis.
steps.say: The kidney hallmark in all ANCA vasculitides is pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis. Capillary wall necrosis allows fibrin and blood to leak into Bowman capsule. The leaked fibrin stimulates parietal epithelial cells and monocytes to proliferate into cellular crescents that crush the glomerular tuft. The term pauci-immune means that immunofluorescence shows virtually no antibody or complement deposition, cleanly separating ANCA vasculitis from immune complex diseases like lupus and anti-GBM Goodpasture disease.

steps.tx: Thromboangiitis obliterans, also known as Buerger disease, is a distinct non-atherosclerotic, segmental, inflammatory vasculitis that predominantly targets small and medium arteries and veins of the distal upper and lower extremities (tibial, plantar, and radial vessels). The disease occurs almost exclusively in **young heavy tobacco smokers**, usually presenting before forty-five years of age. Pathogenesis is driven by direct endothelial toxicity or delayed hypersensitivity to tobacco constituents, inducing acute segmental panarteritis characterized by inflammatory occlusive thrombosis that spares the internal elastic lamina.
steps.say: Buerger disease, or thromboangiitis obliterans, is a non-atherosclerotic vasculitis of small and medium distal extremity vessels seen almost exclusively in heavy cigarette smokers under age forty-five. Tobacco chemicals trigger an intense cellular panarteritis that generates an occlusive inflammatory clot inside the lumen. A critical histological invariant is that despite dense inflammation inside the clot, the arterial wall architecture and internal elastic lamina remain completely intact.

left.title: Buerger Disease (TAO)
points: Exclusively affects young heavy cigarette smokers (<45 yr)
Segmental cellular panarteritis of tibial and radial vessels
Highly cellular occlusive thrombus with microabscesses
Internal elastic lamina remains completely intact

right.title: Atherosclerotic Peripheral Arterial Disease
points: Affects older individuals (>60 yr) with diabetes and smoking
Primary disease of intimal lipid atheroma and fibrous cap
Extensive calcification and disruption of internal media
Targets large femoral, popliteal, and aortoiliac vessels

steps.tx: Histopathological examination of acute Buerger disease reveals a unique, highly cellular luminal thrombus that completely occludes the vascular lumen. Within the thrombus, neutrophils aggregate to form **suppurative microabscesses surrounded by multinucleated giant cells**, with extensive organization and recanalization over time. In stark contrast to necrotizing vasculitides like polyarteritis nodosa, the arterial wall architecture and internal elastic lamina remain remarkably preserved. Furthermore, the inflammatory process characteristically extends into adjacent companion veins and nerves, creating dense fibrous encasement of the neurovascular bundle.
steps.say: Under the microscope, Buerger disease shows an acute cellular thrombus filling the artery. In the center of the clot, neutrophils collect into microabscesses surrounded by multinucleated giant cells. In striking contrast to other vasculitides, there is no fibrinoid necrosis and the internal elastic lamina remains undamaged. The inflammation routinely spills over into the adjacent companion vein and nerve, binding the entire neurovascular bundle in dense fibrous tissue.

rows: Distal tibial and radial arteries, veins, nerves
Buerger uniquely involves veins and nerves
Absence of wall necrosis confirms Buerger
Complete permanent cessation of all tobacco
Immunosuppressants are completely ineffective in TAO

steps.tx: The clinical progression of Buerger disease produces severe distal ischemic manifestations. Patients present with severe instep arch claudication, Raynaud phenomenon, and superficial migratory thrombophlebitis of cutaneous veins. As vascular occlusion becomes complete, excruciating ischemic rest pain develops, followed by non-healing chronic ischemic ulcers and dry **gangrenous digital autoamputation** of toes and fingers. The only known effective intervention that halts disease progression and prevents major limb amputation is total, permanent cessation of all tobacco and nicotine products.
steps.say: Buerger disease manifests clinically with foot arch claudication, Raynaud phenomenon, and tender, red streaks from superficial migratory thrombophlebitis. As distal vessels thrombose completely, patients develop agonizing rest pain that prevents sleep. Fingers and toes become black, dry, and necrotic, leading to spontaneous autoamputation. There is only one effective treatment: the patient must stop all tobacco use permanently. Immunosuppressants and vasodilators fail if smoking continues.

left.title: Clinical Hallmarks of Buerger Disease
points: Severe instep arch claudication and rest pain
Superficial migratory thrombophlebitis of veins
Raynaud phenomenon with cold-induced cyanosis
Ulceration and dry black gangrene of digits

right.title: Essential Management Strategy
points: Complete and permanent smoking cessation is mandatory
Avoid all nicotine replacements (patches, e-cigarettes)
Local wound care and pain control with prostaglandins
Corticosteroids and immunosuppressants are ineffective

quiz.q: Which ANCA pattern and target antigen is identified in over 90% of active cases of granulomatosis with polyangiitis?
options: p-ANCA directed against bactericidal permeability-increasing protein (BPI)
Atypical ANCA directed against neutrophil lactoferrin
quiz.explain: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is strongly associated with diffuse cytoplasmic c-ANCA staining directed against proteinase-3 (PR3).

quiz.q: What histopathological feature distinguishes Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) from other systemic necrotizing vasculitides?
options: Highly cellular luminal thrombi with microabscesses while preserving the internal elastic lamina
Transmural fibrinoid necrosis destroying the internal elastic lamina of medium arteries
Extensive granulomatous Aschoff bodies with central fibrinoid collagen necrosis
Marked myxomatous degeneration of the media with pooling of acid glycosaminoglycans
quiz.explain: Buerger disease is characterized by highly cellular occlusive thrombi containing microabscesses and multinucleated giant cells, while the underlying internal elastic lamina remains intact.

quiz.q: What microscopic feature explains the term pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis in ANCA-associated vasculitis?
options: Direct immunofluorescence demonstrates an absence or paucity of immunoglobulin and complement deposition
The total white blood cell count in peripheral blood is severely reduced under 1000 / uL
Glomerular lesions lack any cellular proliferation or macrophage infiltration
Serum complement C3 and C4 levels are persistently elevated ten-fold above baseline
quiz.explain: Pauci-immune refers to the absence or extreme scarcity of antibody (IgG) and complement deposition on direct immunofluorescence, distinguishing it from immune complex GN.
